stem: Carbon monoxide gas, $\text{CO(g)}$, and nitrogen gas, $\text{N}_2\text{(g)}$, are both diatomic molecules.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The diagram shows the arrangement of outer electrons in a molecule of $\text{CO(g)}$.

{{figure:pdf_visual_01.png}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State **one** similarity and **one** difference in the way the atoms in a carbon monoxide molecule are bonded together compared to the atoms in a nitrogen molecule.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
The table states the electronegativity values of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen atoms.

|  | C | N | O |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| electronegativity | 2.5 | 3.0 | 3.5 |

Use the electronegativity values and relevant details from the *Data Booklet* to complete the table below.

|  | $\text{N}_2$ | $\text{CO}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| number of electrons per molecule |  |  |
| type(s) of intermolecular (van der Waals') force |  |  |

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
$\text{N}_2\text{(g)}$ is less reactive than $\text{CO(g)}$ even though $\text{N}_2\text{(g)}$ has a lower bond energy than $\text{CO(g)}$.

Suggest why $\text{CO(g)}$ is more reactive than $\text{N}_2\text{(g)}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Both carbon monoxide and nitrogen are gases at room temperature and pressure.

They both behave like ideal gases under certain conditions.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: State the **two** conditions necessary for these two gases to approach ideal gas behaviour.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why $\text{N}_2\text{(g)}$ behaves more like an ideal gas than $\text{CO(g)}$ does at $20.0^\circ\text{C}$ and $101\text{ kPa}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
Calculate the amount, in mol, of pure nitrogen gas which occupies $100\text{cm}^3$ at $101\text{ kPa}$ and $20.0^\circ\text{C}$.

Use relevant information from the *Data Booklet*. Show your working.

Assume nitrogen behaves as an ideal gas.
